title: Number System Fundamentals
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Classification, Properties & Prime Testing

introduction.overview: The number system is the backbone of all quantitative aptitude. This chapter classifies numbers into natural, whole, integer, rational, irrational, prime, and composite — and builds the mental framework needed for every subsequent aptitude topic.
introduction.placementRelevance: Number system classification questions appear in 85%+ of campus placement aptitude tests. Prime testing, unit digit cycles, and digit sum rules are tested directly and as prerequisites for HCF, LCM, and simplification.
introduction.realWorldContext: Binary computing uses base-2 numbers. RSA encryption relies on large prime numbers. Financial systems handle integer and rational arithmetic. Number classification underpins all quantitative engineering work.

learningObjectives: Understand and apply core principles of Number System Fundamentals
Identify the correct problem type and method in Number System Fundamentals
Solve Number System Fundamentals questions within 45–60 seconds using shortcuts
Avoid common calculation traps in Number System Fundamentals

requiredTopics: Basic arithmetic: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division
prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Be comfortable with the four operations and with the idea of a factor and a multiple.

coreDefinitions: Natural Numbers (N): Positive counting numbers {1, 2, 3, 4, …}. Do NOT include 0 or negatives.
Whole Numbers (W): Natural numbers plus zero {0, 1, 2, 3, …}.
Integers (Z): All positives, negatives, and zero {…, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …}.
Rational Numbers: Any number of form p/q where p, q are integers and q ≠ 0. Includes all terminating and repeating decimals.
Irrational Numbers: Cannot be expressed as p/q. Their decimals are non-terminating AND non-repeating. Examples: √2, √3, π, e.
Real Numbers (R): The complete set — all rational AND irrational numbers.
Prime Numbers: Natural numbers > 1 with exactly 2 factors (1 and itself). Only even prime is 2.
Composite Numbers: Natural numbers > 1 with MORE than 2 factors.
Co-prime Pair: Two numbers whose HCF = 1. Example: 8 and 15.
Perfect Square: Integer whose square root is also an integer. Example: 36 = 6².
Number 1: Neither prime nor composite — it has exactly 1 factor.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Numbers form a nested family: N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R. Every prime > 3 is of the form 6k ± 1, but not every 6k ± 1 is prime. Unit digits of powers repeat in cycles of length 1, 2, or 4 depending on the base digit.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Draw five concentric circles labelled Natural → Whole → Integer → Rational → Real (innermost to outermost). Irrational numbers sit in the Real ring but outside Rational. When you see √9 = 3 = 3/1, it IS rational. When you see √5 = 2.2360679…, it is NOT rational — it goes in the irrational zone.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Sum of first n natural numbers
Sum of cubes: 1³ + 2³ + … + n³
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Sum of cubed natural numbers equals square of triangle number.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Primality test upper bound
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Test divisibility by all primes ≤ √N only
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: If N has no prime factor ≤ √N, N is prime.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Checking if any number is prime.

mainNarrative: Every aptitude question involving numbers requires classification first. When you see 51, immediately compute 5+1=6 → divisible by 3 → composite (51 = 3×17). When you see 97, test primes up to √97 ≈ 9.8: try 2, 3, 5, 7 — none divide 97 → prime. This 5-second classification replaces 30 seconds of guessing.

Prime factorization is the key tool underlying HCF, LCM, and factor-counting problems. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that every integer > 1 has a unique prime factorization. This uniqueness is why 1 cannot be prime — including 1 as prime would break uniqueness (12 = 2²×3 = 1×2²×3 = 1²×2²×3 = …).

Unit digits of powers follow predictable cycles. The unit digit of 2ⁿ cycles through {2, 4, 8, 6} with period 4. The unit digit of 3ⁿ cycles through {3, 9, 7, 1}. The unit digit of 7ⁿ cycles through {7, 9, 3, 1}. For 4ⁿ: {4, 6} (period 2). For 9ⁿ: {9, 1} (period 2). For 0, 1, 5, 6: unit digit is always the same regardless of the power. To find unit digit of 7^63: 63 mod 4 = 3 → 3rd element of {7,9,3,1} = 3.

Perfect squares have a unit digit restriction: they can ONLY end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, or 9. If a number ends in 2, 3, 7, or 8, it is definitively NOT a perfect square — no calculation needed. This eliminates options in MCQs in under 3 seconds.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why 1 is Neither Prime Nor Composite
deepDiveAspects.content: Primes have exactly 2 factors; composites have ≥ 3. The number 1 has exactly 1 factor (itself). It fits neither category. More importantly, if 1 were prime, the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (every integer > 1 has a unique prime factorization) would be violated — you could always insert extra 1s into any factorization.

deepDiveAspects.title: Unit Digit Cycles — Full Reference
deepDiveAspects.content: Digit 2: cycle {2,4,8,6}, period 4. Digit 3: {3,9,7,1}, period 4. Digit 4: {4,6}, period 2. Digit 7: {7,9,3,1}, period 4. Digit 8: {8,4,2,6}, period 4. Digit 9: {9,1}, period 2. Digits 0,1,5,6: unit digit constant. Method: compute exponent mod period; if remainder=0, use last element of cycle. Example: 2^100: 100 mod 4 = 0 → use 4th element = 6. So unit digit of 2^100 is 6.

problemVariations.description: Classify numbers as prime, composite, rational, irrational, or perfect square.

solvedExamples.title: Finding Unit Digit of a Large Power
solvedExamples.question: What is the unit digit of 3^74?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Unit digit of 3^n follows cycle {3, 9, 7, 1} with period 4.

steps.title: Identify cycle for base 3
steps.explanation: 3¹ ends 3, 3² ends 9, 3³ ends 7, 3⁴ ends 1, 3⁵ ends 3 — cycle {3,9,7,1}, length 4.

steps.title: Find position via modulo
steps.explanation: 74 ÷ 4 = 18 remainder 2. So position = 2nd element of cycle.

steps.title: Read answer
steps.explanation: 2nd element of {3,9,7,1} = 9. Unit digit of 3^74 is 9.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Power unit digits repeat in fixed-length cycles. Mod finds position without computing the full power.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: If remainder = 0, use the LAST element of the cycle, not the first.

solvedExamples.title: Counting Primes Between 50 and 80
solvedExamples.question: How many prime numbers are there between 50 and 80?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Test each odd number: check divisibility by primes ≤ √N.

steps.title: Skip all evens
steps.explanation: All even numbers > 2 are composite. Candidates: 51,53,55,57,59,61,63,67,69,71,73,79.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Testing divisibility only up to √N is sufficient — any composite N must have a factor ≤ √N.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Including 51 (=3×17) or 57 (=3×19) which appear prime at first glance.

solvedExamples.title: Unit digit of a sum of powers
solvedExamples.question: Find the unit digit of 7^2023 + 3^2024.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Unit digits of powers repeat in a cycle of 4 (for 2, 3, 7, 8).

steps.title: Cycle for 7
steps.explanation: Unit digits of 7¹, 7², 7³, 7⁴ are 7, 9, 3, 1, and then repeat.

steps.title: Position of 2023 in the cycle
steps.explanation: 2023 ÷ 4 leaves remainder 3, so the unit digit of 7^2023 is the third in the cycle: 3.

steps.title: Cycle for 3
steps.explanation: Unit digits of 3¹ to 3⁴ are 3, 9, 7, 1. 2024 ÷ 4 leaves remainder 0, so the unit digit of 3^2024 is the fourth in the cycle: 1.

steps.title: Add the unit digits
steps.explanation: 3 + 1 = 4, so the unit digit of the sum is 4.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Only the unit digits matter for the unit digit of a sum, and each power cycles through four unit digits.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Treating a remainder of 0 as the first element of the cycle instead of the last.

shortcutMethods.title: Number System Speed Techniques

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Manually divide by 2, 3, 5, 7… to test primality for each candidate number.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Unit digit cycle (3 seconds per power). Digit sum for composite check (2 seconds). √N limit for primality (under 10 seconds). Together: classify any number in under 15 seconds.

rulesForApplication: All primes > 3 are of form 6k±1 — use to filter candidates before testing.
Perfect squares end only in 0,1,4,5,6,9. If unit digit is 2,3,7,8 → instantly NOT a perfect square.
For unit digit of power: (exponent mod period) → index into cycle. If result = 0, use last element.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: 1 has only 1 factor; primes need exactly 2.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Rational = terminating OR repeating decimal. Irrational = non-terminating AND non-repeating.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring 2 as the only even prime
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Students search for primes only among odds.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Always include 2 when counting or listing primes.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Prime/composite MCQs: eliminate 1 (neither), all evens > 2, multiples of 3 using digit sum. Typically reduces to 1 candidate.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Classify first, calculate second. Classification eliminates 2–3 options without any arithmetic.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Number classification is the opening filter in TCS iON, AMCAT, and CoCubes screening tests.

summaryBullets: N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R. Irrationals ⊂ R but ∉ Q.
1 is neither prime nor composite. Only even prime = 2.
Test primality: check primes up to √N only.

keyTakeaways: Number classification (prime/composite/rational/irrational) is the most tested subtopic in number systems.
Unit digit cycles eliminate large-power computation entirely — learn all cycles before your first mock test.
Always test primality by checking divisors up to √N only — this halves the work.
selfCheckQuestions: Without a calculator, is 127 prime? Show method.
